entries.clue: Invent a herb (4)

blocks.note: to coin a new word or phrase
a common garden herb used in sauces and tea

annotation.walkthrough: Two short definitions sit side by side with no wordplay: coining a word and a kitchen herb share one name.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: to mint a phrase is to invent it, and mint is the familiar herb.

entries.clue: Dodgy stimulator for agents of unwelcome change (10)

indicatorNotes.Dodgy: dodgy means unsound or broken, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A dubious device is blamed for making things worse.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole answer is in one word, a neat pairing of something that boosts with something that damages.
annotation.definitionFit: Those who mutilate bring about a change to something that nobody wanted.

entries.clue: Tangled knotweed? No, only if necessary (4-2-4)

annotation.definitionNote: need-to-know is used adjectivally, as in 'on a need-to-know basis', which the phrase paraphrases

indicatorNotes.Tangled: tangled letters are twisted out of order

annotation.surface: A gardener faced with invasive knotweed decides to deal with it only when forced to.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'No' make the surface read as a conversation about weeding, but the NO is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Information given on a need-to-know basis is shared only when it is necessary.

entries.clue: What may be seen in Manhattan is a film about greed (4,6)

annotation.definition: What may be seen in Manhattan

blocks.clueFragment: What may be seen in Manhattan
blocks.note: the financial district's street in lower Manhattan
Oliver Stone's 1987 film, home of 'greed is good'

annotation.surface: A tourist note that a film set in New York is about greed.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves point at the same place: the real street in New York and the film named after it, whose villain Gordon Gekko declares that greed is good.
annotation.definitionFit: Wall Street is a street in Manhattan and the title of a well-known film about greed.

entries.clue: After injection of iodine, a thorax is most sore (7)

indicatorNotes.After injection of: an injection puts something inside, so I goes into A CHEST

blocks.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine

annotation.surface: A medical note that after an iodine injection the patient's chest hurts most.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes the injection sound like treatment; it is the instruction to put I inside CHEST, after the leading A.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to ache is to be sore, and the superlative ending matches 'most'.

entries.clue: Large prison officers failing to open smallish rooms (7)

indicatorNotes.failing to open: the officers' word loses the letter that would open it

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: Big prison guards cannot unlock the doors of some small rooms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Failing to open' looks like a stuck cell door, and it removes the opening letter W from WARDERS.
annotation.definitionFit: A larder is a small room or cupboard for storing food.

entries.clue: Leading lady to see where appetisers appear (3,2,3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: top of the bill names the star act, here a person

blocks.note: the star performer, named first on a theatre poster
starters are listed first on a restaurant check

annotation.surface: A night out: a show with a star, then a restaurant with starters.
annotation.walkthrough: The theatre bill (the poster listing the acts) and the restaurant bill share a name, and both put the headline item at the top.
annotation.definitionFit: The performer at the top of the bill is the headline act, the one everyone comes to see.

entries.clue: Disasters Leonidas dodged regularly (4)

indicatorNotes.dodged regularly: every other letter is dodged, so only alternate letters remain

annotation.surface: The Spartan king Leonidas repeatedly escaped catastrophe.
annotation.walkthrough: Leonidas is the Spartan king who died at Thermopylae, so the surface has irony, but he is only a string of letters here.
annotation.definitionFit: An end, in the sense of a violent death or ruin, is a disaster.

entries.clue: Country 15? (4)

blocks.note: cross-reference to 15 across, read as food ordered to carry away

annotation.walkthrough: The second definition is a cross-reference: 15 across is TAKEOUT, and a takeout order is one 'to go'. The question mark admits the two-word reading.
annotation.definitionFit: Togo is a country in West Africa, and TO GO is how takeout food is ordered.

entries.clue: We’re told of SE Asians’ connections (4)

indicatorNotes.We’re told: what we are told is heard, so the answer sounds like the wordplay

blocks.note: Thais, people of Thailand in Southeast Asia

annotation.surface: A report about the links between people in Southeast Asia.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe on 'Asians’' makes the surface read as a possessive; it is just the plural sounded out.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: bonds or links between people, as in family ties.

entries.clue: Goth prayed desperately for source of support (7,3)

indicatorNotes.desperately: desperate action is wild, so the letters are thrown about

annotation.surface: A troubled Goth prays hard for help.
annotation.walkthrough: The Goth wants help in the surface and gets it in the answer, an animal brought in to comfort people.
annotation.definitionFit: A therapy dog is brought to hospitals and schools to comfort and support people.

entries.clue: Funny, mirthful Noel, OK? (3-2-3-4)

indicatorNotes.Funny: funny means odd, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a cheerful comedian called Noel is actually any good.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Funny' and 'mirthful' both read as praise for a comic, and 'OK?' looks like a question to him; it is the definition, OK in the sense of merely adequate.
annotation.definitionFit: Something run-of-the-mill is ordinary, just OK; the question mark flags the loose fit.

entries.clue: Greens’ constituent circulated cute leaflet (7,4)

indicatorNotes.circulated: letters sent round are moved into a new order

annotation.surface: A local member of the Green Party hands round an appealing leaflet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greens’ constituent' reads as a voter for the Green Party; it means one part of a plate of salad greens.
annotation.definitionFit: Part for whole: salad greens are made of leaves, and this is one of them.

entries.clue: Everyman regularly gets into these arguments (10)

blocks.note: Everyman is the setter of this weekly puzzle
split as two words: angry words exchanged in a row

annotation.surface: The setter admits to getting into rows often.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman is this puzzle's setter and appears in the Observer every week, so he is regularly in these puzzles. 'Regularly' is not taking alternate letters here.
annotation.definitionFit: Cross words exchanged in anger make an argument, and Everyman's grids appear weekly.

entries.clue: Incites, in middle of open court, displays of fury (10)

indicatorNotes.in middle of: only the letters in the middle of the phrase are taken

blocks.note: the middle five of OPENCOURT: op-ENCOU-rt

annotation.surface: Someone stirs up angry scenes in the middle of a public court hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Open court' reads as a legal term; it is simply nine letters whose centre runs across the word break.
annotation.definitionFit: To encourage someone to act can be to incite them.

entries.clue: Murder a pizza? (7)

blocks.note: a meal bought to eat elsewhere; the question mark says a pizza is only an example

annotation.surface: A gangster's order that could be a hit or a dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: The verb 'take out' is gangster slang for kill; the noun is the delivery meal.
annotation.definitionFit: To take someone out is to murder them, and a pizza is a typical takeout.

entries.clue: Very hot Norwegians, A-ha: randy (to some extent) (7)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: only part of the phrase is used, so the answer is inside it

annotation.surface: The Norwegian pop band A-ha are said to be hot and lustful.
annotation.walkthrough: A-ha, the Norwegian band behind 'Take On Me', make the surface plausible; the hyphen and punctuation are ignored in reading the letters through.
annotation.definitionFit: Saharan heat, like that of the Sahara desert, is extreme.

entries.clue: List includes duck – but you want another bird … (7)

indicatorNotes.includes: the list holds the duck inside it

blocks.note: a roster is a list of names
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O

annotation.surface: A list includes a duck, but the reader asks for a different bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is a bird in the surface, which is why the definition says 'another bird', but in the wordplay it is a cricket score of zero, O. The ellipsis leads on into 19 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male chicken, a different bird from a duck.

entries.clue: Cooked but not good: dotted with holes (7)

indicatorNotes.but not: the letter named after it is left out

annotation.surface: Some food was cooked badly and came out full of holes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not good' reads as a verdict on the cooking; it is an instruction to delete G from GRIDDLED.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: perforated all over, as a riddle, an old word for a coarse sieve, is.

entries.clue: … a small company, and you want credit note up-front? Sauce! (7)

indicatorNotes.up-front: the credit note goes at the front of the rest

blocks.note: a tab is a running record of credit at a bar
S = small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: Continuing from 17 across: someone in a small firm wants an advance on credit, which is cheek.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 17 across. 'Sauce!' with its exclamation mark reads as 'What cheek!'; it is the definition, the hot sauce.
annotation.definitionFit: Tabasco is a brand of hot pepper sauce.

entries.clue: Lad caught by Dorothy’s dog somewhere in N America (7)

indicatorNotes.caught by: the lad is held inside the dog's name

blocks.note: Toto, Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz

annotation.surface: A boy is grabbed by Toto, the dog from The Wizard of Oz, somewhere in America.
annotation.walkthrough: Dorothy and her dog point to Kansas, but the city is in Canada; any boy's name can stand for 'lad'.
annotation.definitionFit: Toronto is a city in Canada, so in North America.

entries.clue: Cockney retained her provision for baking – and something for liqueurs? (11)

indicatorNotes.Cockney: a Cockney speaker drops the H, so the words are heard in that accent

blocks.note: HELD HER with Cockney dropped Hs, then flour, a baker's staple

annotation.surface: A Londoner kept back her baking supplies, with a nod to making liqueurs.
annotation.walkthrough: Cockney is the London working-class accent known for dropping H, so 'held her flour' comes out as the answer. The question mark marks the definition as an example.
annotation.definitionFit: Elderflowers are used to flavour cordials and liqueurs such as St-Germain.

entries.clue: Tosses in a turgid offhand prècis … finally (4)

indicatorNotes.finally: each word gives its final letter

blocks.note: the final letters of A turgiD offhanD prècisS

annotation.surface: A writer throws a few things into a dull, careless summary at the end.
annotation.walkthrough: The single-letter word 'a' counts: its last letter is its only letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To toss something in is to add it, as when adding an extra.

entries.clue: America is a revolutionary, enormous mass of land (4)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution turns things round, so the letters run backwards

annotation.surface: A statement that America is a radical, vast continent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as describing America's history, and it turns the whole string round.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the largest continent is the most enormous landmass there is.

entries.clue: Thomas perhaps embracing trendy field of research (10)

blocks.note: Thomas was one of the twelve disciples

annotation.surface: Someone called Thomas takes up a fashionable area of study.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thomas perhaps' is a definition by example: Doubting Thomas was one of Jesus's twelve followers. The surface makes Thomas sound like a student picking a subject.
annotation.definitionFit: Academic sense: a branch of learning, such as a field in which research is done.

entries.clue: ‘A bore’? Tolkien creature? That’s not on (4)

indicatorNotes.That’s not on: the letters ON are not there

blocks.note: Smaug in The Hobbit is a dragon

annotation.surface: Someone calls a Tolkien monster boring and complains that it is unacceptable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That's not on' is the British phrase for 'that is unacceptable', and it removes ON from DRAGON.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: something tedious is a drag, just as it is a bore.

entries.clue: Daffy old boater’s one swinging more than one way (6,4)

annotation.definition: one swinging more than one way

indicatorNotes.Daffy: daffy means scatty, so the letters are scattered

annotation.surface: A silly old boating man is a swinger.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S in 'boater’s' looks like 'boater is' and supplies the S of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A stable door is split into top and bottom halves that swing open independently.

entries.clue: Judas Iscariot, within: unaltered (2,2)

indicatorNotes.within: the answer is inside the words

annotation.surface: Judas Iscariot is inside and unchanged.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the break between the two names.
annotation.definitionFit: Goods sold as is are sold unaltered, in their present state.
